The model was working. That was the confusing part. We were pulling fields out of enterprise documents at 90%+ accuracy. By every metric we’d agreed to measure, the thing was done. And it still wasn’t ready for production. It took me too long to see why. The problem wasn’t the model. The problem was that I’d been managing the model as if it were the product. Part 1: The three approaches For this document automation use case, we ran three tracks in parallel — traditional ML, a vision-based model, and OCR + LLM. Not because we couldn’t decide, but because customers won’t wait a year for the perfect model. Traditional ML gave us that 90%+ number. On our evaluation set. Which turned out to be far cleaner than what production sent us: scans photocopied three times, layouts nobody anticipated, ground truth that was inconsistent because two teams had labelled it differently. Then latency under parallel load — a problem with nothing to do with accuracy and everything to do with whether anyone can use the thing. The model hadn’t got worse. The environment had changed, and our metric was never measuring the environment. Vision-based beat it on extraction quality in many scenarios. It also failed differently — pulling the right values off the page while missing something important about how the document was structured. OCR + LLM was the least sophisticated and the most adaptable. A new document type meant adjusting prompts, not running a full modelling cycle. None of them won outright. That was the most useful thing we learned. Part 2: What the PM actually does If there’s no winner on the leaderboard, someone has to make the call anyway. That’s the job. It comes down to three things. Deciding which trade-off the customer actually feels. Higher accuracy → Can mean higher latency or compute cost More capability → Can mean higher cost per document More flexibility → Can mean more governance challenges and less predictability Better benchmark performance → Doesn’t always mean better reliability on messy production data For a finance team closing month-end, two seconds of latency is invisible and one wrong invoice total is a crisis. For a high-volume intake queue, that ranking flips entirely. Same model, opposite decision. Designing what happens when the AI is wrong. Not if . At 90% accuracy on a document with 20 fields, being wrong is the expected case for almost every document. So: Can the user tell it’s wrong, or does a bad value arrive looking exactly as confident as a good one? Can they fix it in two seconds, or does it take a support ticket? Do we capture the correction, or does it die in the user’s head? Does anything improve because of it? None of those are model questions. All of them are product questions. Building the loop that keeps it alive. Flexibility isn’t free. Prompts drift. New edge cases surface. Customer feedback rewrites the requirement you thought was settled. So the product needs a path for real usage to reach whoever can act on it, without waiting for an engineering release. Traditional software doesn’t get worse when the world changes around it. AI products do. That’s the part nobody warns you about. Part 3: The lesson I used to ask: which solution performs best? Now I ask: which solution creates the best customer outcome under our real constraints? The second question is harder. There’s no leaderboard for it, and no eval run settles it. It needs someone who understands the technology, the customer and the constraints well enough to make a call a benchmark can’t make for them. That’s the job. The model is a component. The workflow is the product. The customer outcome is the goal. First in Lessons from Building Enterprise AI Products — practical product lessons from building AI for real enterprise problems. If you’ve hit the gap between a model that works and a product that ships, I’d like to hear how you handled it.
